name: Particle Text
blurb: A word rasterised into a grid of small lights, with a hole the pointer carries through it. The particles never scatter: each one keeps a home cell in the glyph and a critically damped spring pulls it back, so the word stays legible and the hole is the only thing that moves. The arrow on the stage is the library's own User Cursor, demonstrating it until a real hand arrives.

The idea comes from React Bits Pro, whose source is paid and gated and whose licence (2.4) forbids putting the Product in a repository or making it available to third parties; this repo is public and ships dist/ as a reusable bundle, so no Pro source may enter it. Nothing was copied - the sampler, the spring, the rim target and the tour are written here against a screen recording, and sourceUrl points at the docs page for provenance only.

Four decisions are load-bearing. The hole is a TARGET, not a force: a particle inside the radius is given a target on the rim, so the inside empties completely and the boundary draws itself - a repulsive force moves each particle by however long it has been in the field, which blows the word into a cloud and never produces an edge. The stage is dark in both themes, like Vortex's and Data Transfer's, because a field of small lights only exists against a dark ground. Tech Blue is in the palette and is deliberately not the mixed default, since #052975 on #070d1a is not a light - Innovation Blue carries the word, with Smart Green and Performance Purple as a minority. And the arrow is the library's User Cursor, mounted, with its pill empty: the standing rule is that any entry whose point is a pointer demonstrates it with that one arrow, and a name pill on a demo that is not about a person is a label with nothing to say.

height.note: the stage. Both hosts clamp a component's mount to the card, so this only bites when the entry is used on its own.

text.note: empty takes the element's own text, which is the usual case - the word stays in the DOM for a screen reader either way. Pass it only when the visible markup cannot be the word.

weight.note: the hub's heaviest weight. A light weight does not survive the sampler: at a 5px grid a hairline stroke lands on one cell in three and the word comes out dotted.

family.note: empty inherits the page's font, which is what you want - this entry never loads one. The raster is rebuilt on document.fonts.ready, because sampling before the webfont arrives samples the fallback's shapes and the word silently comes out in the wrong typeface.

gap.note: the grid step. In px rather than a ratio, because the picture IS a pixel grid - scaling it with the stage would make a card and a hero two different textures.

dot.note: the square drawn at each cell. dot < gap is what leaves the lattice visible; at dot = gap the word is a solid block and the effect is invisible until the pointer arrives.

max.note: particle cap. `gap` is widened until the count fits, so a long word on a wide hero costs the same as a short one.

fillX.note: how much of the width the word may take. Two numbers because a long word is limited by the width and a short one by the height; the smaller of the two sizes is the one used.

fillY.note: how much of the height the word may take, measured on the ink rather than the line box - a word with no descender sits visibly low when it is centred on the line box instead.

maxSize.note: cap on the font size; 0 is no cap. For a one- or two-letter word on a wide stage, where filling the width would make a single glyph the size of the section.

radius.note: the hole. Judge it against the cap height, not the stage: a radius under the word's own height reads as a smudge rather than as something being carried through it.

swirl.note: how far the rim target slides sideways. It is what makes the pile streak tangentially instead of stacking; at 0 the rim is a clean ring and reads as a stencil.

push.note: the spring's time constant while a particle is displaced, off the duration scale. The hole has to open as fast as the pointer moves or it trails the arrow.

settle.note: the time constant on the way home. Deliberately four times `push`: the slow return is the whole of the wake, and matching the two makes the hole look like a hole punched in paper rather than carried through a field.

twinkle.note: the shimmer's loop length. A loop, so an option rather than a token - the duration scale is for things that start and finish.

sparkle.note: 0-1, how deep the shimmer cuts. A flat field of identical squares reads as a halftone print; a per-particle phase makes it read as something lit. Past ~0.6 the word starts to flicker rather than breathe.

accent.note: mixed is Innovation Blue carrying the word with Smart Green and Performance Purple as a minority - one hue reads as a logo, four read as confetti. Tech Blue is available and is not the default: #052975 on the near-black stage is not a light.

bg.note: empty keeps the stylesheet's dark stage. Palette colours only, and dark ones - the particles are lights.

seed.note: the tints and the shimmer phases. Seeded and rolled once, so the gallery card and the Video card agree about every particle and a resize does not reshuffle the field.

cursor.note: mount the library's User Cursor and hand it the tour. Off, this is a word waiting for a real pointer.

name.note: the cursor's pill. Empty is the arrow on its own, which is what this wants - the pill is for a demo about a person.

cycle.note: one full figure-eight. A loop length, so an option rather than a token.

autoplay.note: run once it scrolls into view, and stop again when it leaves or the tab is hidden. The last frame stays on the canvas, so a card scrolled back into view already shows the word.

paused.note: stops the loop. The word stays assembled on screen - a paused card shows the content, not an empty stage.

compact.note: the card-sized skin, for a stage under ~200px

notPorted: No click, and no press() on the tour. This is a hover demo: the hole follows the pointer and a click does nothing, so rendering one would be the demo claiming a behaviour the entry does not have. The standing rule is the other way round - an entry about clicking that never shows a click is the failure - and it does not apply to an entry about hovering.

No assemble-on-enter. Flying the particles in from the edges at mount is the obvious opening and it costs the thing the entry is for: the word has to be readable the instant it is on screen, and a card that arrives as a cloud reads as a loading state. The spring is already the entry's whole motion vocabulary; it is spent on the hole.

No image source. Rasterising a photograph rather than a glyph is the same sampler and a different entry - the font fitting, the accessibility span and the per-particle tinting all exist because this one is text. A picture would want none of them.

No WebGL. At the counts this runs (a card is ~500 particles, a hero ~4,000) one ImageData write per frame is cheaper than a context, a program and a buffer upload, and it keeps the entry dependency-free - the hub ships no Three.js and must not grow one for a word.

name: Center Flow
blurb: A lit tile in the middle of a dark stage with eight smaller ones around it, and a pulse of light leaving the centre along every spoke in turn. Each pulse lands on its node, the node answers with a short flash, and the spoke goes quiet again. The hourglass in the hub runs while it happens.

The hub tile and the pulses are always Innovation Blue, never a lightened tint - at a 2px line width on near-black, Tech Blue is not visible, which is the same finding Vortex's field and Globe's land produced, so `accent` moves the SATELLITES instead, where a second hue can do some work. height.note: the stage. Both hosts clamp a component's mount to the card, so this only bites when the entry is used on its own.

nodes.note: the satellites. Six reads as a diagram and twelve as a dial; eight is the count that still leaves room for a flash on each.

spread.note: the node ring's width as a fraction of the stage

ratio.note: the ring's height as a fraction of its width. 1 is a circle, which leaves a gutter at each side of a wide stage; near 0 collapses the fan to a line. The ring is also clamped to the stage's height, so a card never runs its top and bottom nodes off the edge.

centreSize.note: the hub tile at the default 420px stage. Every px option here is scaled by the stage, so a card gets a smaller diagram rather than a cropped one.

nodeSize.note: a satellite tile at the default stage

radius.note: corner radius as a fraction of a tile's size, so the hub lands on the hub's own 15px tile radius and the satellites stay in proportion instead of turning into circles

bow.note: how far a spoke bows off its chord. 0 is a star of straight lines; past about 0.3 the spokes cross one another. One sign for the whole fan, so it turns together rather than mirroring.

cycle.note: one pulse: leave, travel, land, and the gap before the next

travel.note: how much of the cycle the pulse is in flight for. The rest is the gap - without one the spokes are a permanent chain of lights and nothing reads as leaving.

tail.note: the comet's length as a fraction of the spoke. It runs past the far end, so a pulse is swallowed by its node rather than switched off on top of it.

stagger.note: how far the pulses are spread around the fan, in whole cycles. 1 walks the fan once per cycle; 0 fires all eight together.

pulseWidth.note: the pulse's core at its head; it tapers to a third of that at the tail

lineWidth.note: the resting spoke. It is always drawn - the system has to be legible in the gap between pulses, not only while something is travelling.

flash.note: how hard a node answers when a pulse lands, 0-1. The flash is handed to the nodes by the pulse pass rather than worked out twice, so the two can never disagree about when a pulse arrived.

icon.note: the glyph in the hub tile, drawn in code rather than loaded - a font or an SVG here is a second request that can 404 on a page that has already painted

drain.note: the hourglass runs: the sand falls and the glass turns over when it is empty. A still glyph in the middle of eight moving spokes reads as a dead pixel.

glassCycle.note: the glass empties and turns over once. Deliberately not a multiple of `cycle` - when the two line up, the flip always lands on the same spoke and the whole picture picks up a beat.

breathe.note: the hub's halo swells and settles once

glow.note: the halo behind the hub tile. Drawn BEFORE the spokes, so it reads as light coming off the tile rather than as a wash over the diagram.

grid.note: the faint dot field. Not decoration: a plain dark box gives the eye nothing to measure the spokes against, so the fan reads as floating.

gridGap.note: between grid dots, at the default stage

accent.note: the SATELLITES' palette. The hub and the pulses stay Innovation Blue whatever this is - they are the lit part, and a dark hue there is invisible on a near-black ground.

background.note: empty keeps the stylesheet's dark stage

seed.note: the node colours and the field are random but fixed - the same seed lays out identically on both hosts and across every resize

compact.note: the card-sized skin, for a stage under ~200px

name: Data Transfer

height.note: the stage. Both hosts clamp a component's mount to the card, so this only bites when the entry is used on its own.

count.note: how many streams are in the air at once. Under about eight it reads as a few stray lines rather than as traffic; the burnout at the convergence point also scales with it, because that is the one place every stream passes through.

speed.note: how long one stream takes to run its whole path. A loop length, so it is an option rather than a token.

vary.note: the spread of speeds across the streams. 0 runs them in lockstep, which reads as a machine rather than as traffic.

tail.note: how much of the path the shutter was open for, 0-1. This is the exposure: near 0 it is a moving dot, near 1 the whole path is lit at once and nothing appears to move.

width.note: the core at its thickest, at the near end of the path

glow.note: the halo around the core, and the radius the head blooms to

heat.note: how far the core is mixed toward white. A long exposure saturates its own centre, and it is also the only reason Tech Blue is legible on a near-black ground.

arc.note: the direction the fan points away from the convergence point. 0 is right, 90 is down. Aimed down rather than down-left so the fan covers the stage: past about 130 every lane sits on one side of the convergence point and the other half of the frame stays empty for the whole loop.

spread.note: how wide the fan opens. Wide enough to reach both bottom corners, narrow enough that the lanes still read as lanes; past about 120 it turns into a starburst, and 360 gives rays in every direction.

curve.note: how far the paths bend on their way in. 0 is straight rays; the bend is what makes them cross near the convergence point, which is the tangle the effect is recognised by.

vanishX.note: the convergence point across the stage, 0-1

vanishY.note: and down it. Near the top is the road-at-night read; in the middle it is a starburst. Not flush with the edge - the bundle is the subject, and at 0.02 the frame crops it.

direction.note: toward the convergence point or away from it. in is data arriving, which is the default because that is the Continia story - documents coming from everywhere and landing in one place.

accent.note: palette only. mixed is a weighted bag of Innovation Blue, Smart Green and Tech Blue - three hues read as one photograph, four read as a test card. There is no auto: the ground is always dark, so there is nothing for it to follow.

background.note: empty keeps the stylesheet's, which is the hub's own dark canvas. The module reads the resolved colour back off the element, so the stylesheet and the JS can never disagree about what colour the stage is.

bloom.note: the soft head on the leading end of each trail, and the blown-out core at the convergence point. Off is cheaper and reads as a drawn line rather than as a light.

seed.note: the fan is random but fixed - the same seed always lays out the same way, on both hosts and across every resize

autoplay.note: run once it scrolls into view, and stop again when it leaves or the tab is hidden

compact.note: the card-sized skin, for a stage under ~200px

reducedMotion: A photograph, not an empty box. The streams are frozen at their own phases part-way through the run, so what is on screen is exactly one long exposure - which is what the entry is. Nothing loops, no frame is ever requested, and the fade-in is dropped.
notPorted: the reference's own subject. It is a general long-exposure treatment over whatever is behind it; this is one specific picture - light converging on a point - because that is the one that says something about Continia rather than just looking expensive.

accumulation. The obvious build is a translucent wipe over the canvas each frame with a dot moving across it, letting the smear pile up. That trail's length depends on the frame rate, the exposure has to be thrown away and rebuilt on every resize, and pausing freezes a half-built smudge. Here the whole trail is redrawn every frame from a fixed curve, so the picture is a pure function of the clock: framerate-independent, resize-safe, and seekable.
colour as a free value. The source takes any hex; accent here is one of four palette names or mixed, and anything else throws.
copy. The entry keeps whatever children it is given and lays them over the exposure, so the words belong to the page and not to this module.

Nothing was copied - sourceUrl points at the docs page for provenance only.

Three decisions are load-bearing. There is no frame loop: every ring carries one infinite linear rotate animation and every face the same animation reversed, so the main thread does nothing once the DOM is built. That is a gallery decision as much as a brand one - sixty entries share a page, and several of them are already painting canvases while you scroll past.

The default face is a drawn silhouette in a brand tint rather than a photograph, for the same reason the reel's demo is numbered boxes: an entry whose demo needs particular image files breaks when they move. A silhouette and not a monogram, because a letter makes a claim about who the person is and this is scenery.

And the stage is dark in BOTH themes, as Globe's and Vortex's are: these are lit objects, and a lit object on a light ground is a flat shape.

rings.note: how many concentric rings, 1-8. The count of faces is not set here - it comes off each ring's own circumference.

reach.note: the outermost ring's radius as a fraction of HALF THE LONGER axis of the stage. Over 1 the ring runs off the top and bottom and is clipped, which is the look: a ring fitted to the shorter axis leaves the sides empty and reads as a medallion.
